questions.q: What is the root cause that makes an application vulnerable to SQL injection?
options: Untrusted input is concatenated directly into a query string instead of being bound as data
The application uses MySQL instead of PostgreSQL
The web server is running an outdated version of TLS
The application does not use HTTPS
questions.explain: SQL injection exists the moment user input is concatenated into the SQL text itself. Parameterized queries fix this by binding input as data, never as part of the query string.

questions.q: A tester submits a payload like "' AND SLEEP(5) --" and observes the response take noticeably longer when the injected condition is true, with no error message or extra data returned. What technique is this?
options: Error-based injection
UNION-based injection
Time-based blind injection
DOM-based injection
questions.explain: Time-based blind injection confirms the flaw indirectly: when the app shows no errors or extra data, a payload like SLEEP(5) makes the response visibly slower only when the injected condition evaluates true.

questions.q: Why is "the app uses an ORM" not sufficient by itself to conclude an application is safe from SQL injection?
options: ORMs are always vulnerable regardless of configuration
ORMs make it easy to skip parameter binding in places like raw SQL escape hatches, dynamic ORDER BY clauses, or stored procedures with dynamic SQL
ORMs only work with NoSQL databases, not SQL
ORMs disable all input validation by default
questions.explain: A tester verifies every input path actually uses parameter binding, including overlooked paths an ORM makes easy to bypass — raw-query escape hatches, dynamic column/table names, and stored procedures building SQL dynamically.

questions.q: What distinguishes stored XSS from reflected XSS?
options: Stored XSS only affects the attacker's own browser, never other users
Stored XSS requires no authentication of any kind to exploit
Stored XSS cannot be confirmed with an alert() payload
The payload in stored XSS is saved server-side and executes for every user who later views the stored content, rather than requiring a crafted link to be clicked
questions.explain: Reflected XSS rides in the request and affects only someone who clicks a crafted link; stored XSS is saved server-side (e.g. a comment field) and executes for every subsequent viewer, which is why its impact is typically far higher.

questions.q: What must a tester do with a stored XSS payload after confirming the vulnerability during an authorized engagement?
options: Leave it in place so the client can see it in the final report walkthrough
Clean it up, since leaving a live payload sitting in the client's production data is itself a problem the tester doesn't want to cause
Immediately disclose it publicly to pressure the client into fixing it
Nothing — stored XSS payloads are automatically removed by the browser
questions.explain: Stored payloads must be cleaned up after confirmation. Leaving a live XSS payload sitting in a client's production data would itself create a real security issue the engagement caused rather than just found.
